front: The five levels of agile planning
back: Product vision, product roadmap, release plan, iteration plan, daily plan. Each is more detailed and shorter-range than the one above.
A high-level timeline of the release, typically 3 to 6 months, based on the roadmap and vision. Sets the number of iterations in the release.
Shows the expected sequence of major deliverables or capabilities over time. Owned by the product owner and replanned as things change.
An ordered list of work to be done, often written as user stories and prioritized by the business.
Epic: a large body of work spanning iterations. Feature: a capability made of related stories. User story: fits in one iteration. Task: a piece of work within a story.
A brief description of an outcome for a specific user, which is a promise for a conversation to clarify details.
As a (role), I want (goal), so that (benefit).
Card (short written story), conversation (details worked out by talking), confirmation (acceptance criteria).
Independent, negotiable, valuable, estimable, small, testable.
The specific conditions a story must meet to be accepted.

front: Definition of ready vs definition of done
back: Ready: the story has everything the team needs to start. Done: the criteria a deliverable must meet to be ready for customer use.
A unit for the relative effort needed to implement a user story. Not hours.
Estimating items by comparing them with each other. Fast; trades some accuracy for speed.
Each member privately picks a card; all cards are revealed together; high and low explain; the team re-votes until it converges.

front: Why reveal planning poker cards at the same time?
back: To avoid anchoring: the first number spoken pulling everyone else's estimate toward it.
Sizing items as XS, S, M, L, XL. Quick, for early or large-scale estimating.
Placing items in groups of similar size. Fast for a large number of items.
The rate at which the team produces, validates and accepts deliverables per interval. Usually story points completed per iteration.

front: Can velocity be compared between teams?
back: No. Story points are specific to each team.
Iterations needed = remaining story points ÷ average velocity.
How much the team can take on in the coming iteration, given who is available.
A meeting to clarify backlog items, acceptance criteria and effort for the upcoming iteration. The team decides how much it takes on.
Progressive elaboration and reprioritization of the backlog to get items ready for upcoming iterations.
A visual way of organizing stories to see high-value features over time, find gaps in the backlog and plan releases.
A short, fixed period in which work is to be completed. Time is fixed; scope varies.
A regular rhythm of activities through the project.
A timeboxed story or task created to research a question or resolve a problem.
A set-up iteration before development: environment, initial backlog, team agreements.

front: A story is too big for one iteration. What do you do?
back: Split it into smaller stories, each still valuable.

front: Do half-finished stories count toward velocity?
back: No. Only stories that are finished and accepted count.
